text: 1. Naming the accusation as a symptom of the disease before offering anything practical is what helps most. Caregivers who hear first that this is a known part of the disease, and not about them, are better able to use what comes next. Asking whether the accusations cluster at a particular time of day often points to late afternoon. Keeping a small amount of cash somewhere the person can find it themselves lets the search end without a confrontation.

2. Arguing the merits of the service tends not to work with caregivers who have refused help more than once. In one case a daughter caring for her mother had turned down homemaker services three times, having promised years earlier never to let strangers in the house. Asking what her mother would say if she could see how tired she was moved the conversation to the promise instead of the services. She agreed to a two-hour trial visit the following month and kept the service afterward.

3. Caregivers who say they can't leave the person alone are usually right, and offering a group before solving that tends not to land. Raising the respite question first (an adult day program, a neighbor, a grandchild for two hours) makes the group offer usable. Where no respite option exists, a phone or online group has worked better than an in-person one.

4. Declining to answer the placement question directly, while offering to help think it through, has worked better than either answering or deflecting. Asking what a normal day looks like now, and what would have to change to keep going, often leads caregivers to answer their own question while describing the day. Where the question is coming from guilt rather than from an actual decision, that is a different conversation and is better addressed first.

5. Raising a caregiver's own symptom again at a later call, rather than only at the call where they mention it, is what tends to get them to go. A single suggestion to see a doctor has usually not been enough on its own.

6. Contradicting a family who says the person is just getting old has worked less well than asking what they have noticed that seemed different, and writing the examples down as they talk. Offering the list for them to take to the doctor changes what the visit produces.
